newsitem.title: USA: U.S. confirms Russia warned over Iran arms sales.
newsitem.headline: U.S. confirms Russia warned over Iran arms sales.

text.p: Washington issued a diplomatic warning to Moscow about Russian assistance to Iran's missile programme that could threaten U.S. troops in Saudi Arabia, several Gulf allies and Israel, the Los Angeles Times reported on Wednesday.

Quoting senior Clinton administration officials, the newspaper said intelligence reports indicated that Russia recently transferred to Iran technology for the Russian SS-4 missile, which has a range almost three times greater than that of any missile now in Iran's arsenal.

The transfer basically involved detailed instructions on how to construct the missile's delivery system. But the Times quoted Israeli officials as saying it included some parts for an SS-4 missile, which has a range of 1,250 miles (2,010 km).

The diplomatic warning was reportedly issued during talks last week between Vice President Al Gore and visiting Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the United States had raised its concerns over Russian arms sales to Iran at the meeting but he did not know whether the specific issue of SS-4 missiles came up.
"We don't believe that any country should sell arms to Iran ... and I know this issue was raised in the recent Gore-Chernomyrdin proceedings," Burns told reporters.

According to the Times, Chernomyrdin denied that Moscow had authorised transfer of the missile and acknowledged that such action would violate a 1994 pledge by Russian President Boris Yeltsin not to engage in further arms sales to Tehran.
U.S. officials speculated the missile technology could have been transferred to Iran from cash-strapped former Soviet arms producers or complexes, the Times reported.

Since the advent of capitalism in Russia, it was possible for firms to export arms without government knowledge, Burns said. "I have no indication that Russia has violated the pledge made to President Bill Clinton by President Yeltsin."
Yeltsin said in 1994 that Russia felt obliged to proceed with arms sales to Iran that were already subject to contracts but would not engage in new sales of certain types of military equipment.
